While developing a tourism model is an excellent way to save a threatened ecosystem,
not every fishing village has that opportunity. Besides, tourism doesn't create many
jobs. For conservation to work, fishermen need a way to make money while they wait
for their resource to recover. And the conservation efforts need manpower. To this end,
the community of El Manglito has adopted an interesting strategy. Fishermen there
once freely harvested shellfish from the broad, shallow bay west of town. By 2009, very
few were left. With financial support from Noroeste Sustentable, a nonprofit organization
in the neighboring city of La Paz, the fishermen, many of whom were involved in
poaching, turned away from this illegal activity and began managing their resources.
They were paid to watch for poachers and conduct biological surveys to estimate the
amount of shellfish. The first survey estimated that fewer than 100,000 shellfish were
left. Today it's more like 2.3 million.
Ultimately, for conservation to work. community cohesion and trust are essential. In
rural Baja, trust in one’s neighbor can be hard to find, but it’s possible to create it. At
least that’s what a conservation organization called Niparaja is working to achieve.
Niparaja works on sustainable fisheries in an especially desolate region of southeastern
Baja. When Niparaja started working in communities there, it didn’t focus on fishing.
Instead it promoted soccer tournaments. Sponsoring these in tiny towns might seem
like a waste of time and money but it slowly built trust between villages that have
jealously guarded fishing grounds from each other. Next Niparaja took some fishermen
to Cabo Pulmo to see the impact a fishing ban can have on ocean life. Eventually, after
years of discussions, the villages decided to try conservation. Each selected a smail
area and agreed not to fish in it for five years. The areas are not big — the largest is just
under three square miles — but it was a start.
